title: ZBiotics Alternatives: PartySmart, Myrkl, Day Guard and DHM
excerpt: Looking for a ZBiotics alternative? An honest comparison of PartySmart, Myrkl, Day Guard, DHM supplements and drinks, with what each costs, what it targets, and what the evidence really shows.
metaDescription: Honest ZBiotics alternatives compared: PartySmart, Myrkl, Day Guard and DHM. What each targets, cost per night, and what the evidence really shows.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no ZBiotics alternative with clearly better evidence behind it. What you can find are options that are cheaper, easier to take, or built on a different idea. The three brands people most often compare with ZBiotics are PartySmart (an Ayurvedic herbal capsule), Myrkl (a probiotic pill), and products sold as Day Guard. Beyond those, the most common switch is to a DHM supplement, which costs far less per night. There is no good evidence that any of them prevents hangovers, so the smart move is to pick the option whose trade-offs suit you and test it honestly.

**Quick picks:**

| If you want... | Consider | Why |
|---|---|---|
| The cheapest pill to try | PartySmart or plain DHM | A fraction of ZBiotics's per-night cost |
| Another probiotic | Myrkl | The best-known probiotic rival, with one small published trial |
| An option that isn't limited to the gut | DHM (capsule or drink) | Absorbed into the body; most research is in animals |
| The best odds of a better morning | Less alcohol, food, water, sleep | Free, and better supported than any product |

> **This is not medical advice.** This page compares how companies describe their products with the published research we could find. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. None of these products is approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and none of them lowers your blood alcohol enough to make driving safe. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before trying any of them if** you take prescription medicine, are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, or have a weakened immune system (probiotics are not recommended for some people in that group). If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or can't be woken, call 911.

We don't sell ZBiotics, PartySmart, Myrkl, or Day Guard, so there are no links to buy them here. We do earn a commission on some DHM products mentioned later, and we say so where they appear.

## Why People Look for a ZBiotics Alternative

ZBiotics is a real product with a clever idea behind it: a food-safe bacterium, *Bacillus subtilis*, engineered to make an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde in your gut. Acetaldehyde is the toxic chemical your body makes on the way to clearing alcohol. Our full [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) goes through the science in detail. The short version of why people go looking elsewhere comes down to five things.

1. **Price.** At typical retail prices one bottle tends to run about $10 to $15, a bit less on subscription. For someone who goes out once or twice a week, that's hundreds of dollars a year.
2. **It only works in the gut.** Most acetaldehyde is made in your liver, where a probiotic in your intestines can't reach it. So even if ZBiotics works exactly as designed, it can only touch part of the problem.
3. **Acetaldehyde may not be the main cause of a hangover.** By the time most hangovers peak, alcohol and acetaldehyde are largely cleared. Researchers also point to inflammation, poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, and congeners (other chemicals in drinks, especially dark spirits).
4. **Mixed results from real users.** Some people swear by it. Many others, including plenty of people on Reddit, say they couldn't tell a difference.
5. **Format and preference.** It's a drink you have to remember before your first drink. Some people would rather take a capsule, and some simply prefer to avoid a genetically engineered organism.

If one of those is your reason, the right alternative is different. Someone put off by the price needs something cheaper. Someone who doubts the gut-only mechanism needs something that works through a different route. Keep your reason in mind as you read the options.

## How We Judged the Alternatives

Hangover products are hard to compare fairly because almost none of them has strong evidence. A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary remedy reliably prevents or treats hangovers, and later reviews have mostly found small, early studies. So instead of pretending one product "wins," we looked at five practical questions:

- **What's actually in it,** and is the label clear?
- **What is it supposed to do,** and does that make sense given how the body handles alcohol?
- **What human evidence exists,** who paid for it, and did it measure hangover symptoms or something else, like blood alcohol?
- **What does it cost per night** at typical prices?
- **Is there anything to watch for** on safety?

We didn't run our own trials, and we don't claim any product here works for everyone. Where we couldn't find reliable information, we say so.

## PartySmart vs ZBiotics

PartySmart is an herbal capsule from Himalaya Wellness, an Indian company known for Ayurvedic products. It's sold widely online and in many drugstores, and it's one of the cheapest hangover products you'll find.

### What it is

PartySmart is a blend of plant extracts drawn from Ayurvedic tradition. Labels have listed ingredients such as Indian gooseberry (amla) and chicory, among others. The exact recipe can vary by market and over time, so check the current label. The directions are usually one capsule before or while drinking.

### How it's supposed to work

Himalaya says PartySmart helps the body break down acetaldehyde faster and supports the liver. That's the same target ZBiotics names, but by a different route: plant compounds that are absorbed into the body rather than bacteria working in the gut.

### What the evidence shows for PartySmart

The company points to its own research, including studies it says showed lower acetaldehyde levels. As far as we're aware, there is no large, independent, placebo-controlled trial showing PartySmart reduces hangover symptoms. Some of the individual herbs have been studied for liver effects, mostly in animals, but that doesn't tell you what one capsule of this blend does after a night out.

### PartySmart vs ZBiotics at a glance

| | PartySmart | ZBiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Herbal capsule | Engineered probiotic drink |
| **Target** | Acetaldehyde and the liver (per company) | Acetaldehyde in the gut |
| **Cost per night** | Usually around a dollar or less | Roughly $10 to $15 |
| **Independent hangover trials** | None we could find | None we could find |
| **Convenience** | Small capsule, easy to carry | Small bottle, take before drinking |

**Pros:** very cheap, easy to carry, widely available, and the company is established.

**Cons:** the main research is company-backed, multi-herb blends are hard to evaluate, and herbal products can vary in quality. Herbal liver products can occasionally interact with medicines, so check with a pharmacist if you take anything regularly.

**Our take:** if your main problem with ZBiotics is the price, PartySmart is a low-cost experiment. Its evidence isn't better, just cheaper to test.

## Myrkl vs ZBiotics

Myrkl is the closest rival to ZBiotics because it's also a probiotic you take before drinking. It comes from a Swedish company, De Faire Medical, and got a lot of press when it launched in the UK in 2022.

### What it is and how it's supposed to work

Myrkl is a pill containing a blend of probiotic bacterial strains plus vitamins, according to the company. The formula has been described differently over time and across markets, so check the current label. The key difference from ZBiotics is the target. ZBiotics aims at acetaldehyde. Myrkl's pitch is that its bacteria break down **alcohol itself** in the gut, so less of it gets into your blood. The company recommends taking it in advance of drinking, and the published trial had people take it for several days beforehand.

### What the evidence shows for Myrkl

Myrkl has something most hangover products don't: a published human trial. It appeared in *Nutrition and Metabolic Insights* in 2022, was funded by the company, and involved a small group of healthy adults (roughly two dozen). After about a week on the product, participants drank a moderate amount of alcohol, and the researchers reported lower blood alcohol than with a placebo.

That's interesting, but it has real limits:

- **It measured blood alcohol, not hangovers.** It didn't show people felt better the next morning.
- **It was small and company-funded.** Results like this often shrink in larger, independent studies.
- **The alcohol dose was moderate.** A big night out is a different test.
- **Breaking down alcohol in the gut still makes acetaldehyde.** The first step of breaking down alcohol produces exactly the chemical ZBiotics is designed to clear. Making more of it in the gut isn't automatically better.

When Myrkl launched, independent experts quoted in UK coverage also worried that a pill marketed around lower blood alcohol could encourage people to drink more or misjudge how drunk they are. That's a fair concern.

### Myrkl vs ZBiotics at a glance

| | Myrkl | ZBiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **Format** | Pill | Small drink |
| **Target** | Alcohol in the gut | Acetaldehyde in the gut |
| **When to take** | In advance, often for days | Before the first drink |
| **Published human study** | One small company-funded trial on blood alcohol | Mainly company research and testing |
| **Hangover symptoms measured** | No | Not in an independent trial we could find |

**Our take:** Myrkl suits someone who likes the probiotic idea but would rather take a pill. It has slightly more published human data than ZBiotics, but that data answers a different question from the one you care about the morning after. Our guide to [hangover probiotics](/never-hungover/hangover-probiotics) covers both products and ordinary probiotics in more depth.

## Day Guard vs ZBiotics

"Day Guard vs ZBiotics" is a search people make, and we want to be straight about it: we couldn't find consistent, reliable information about what's in products sold under the Day Guard name, who makes them, or any published human research behind them. Names like this are often used by several small sellers on large online marketplaces, and the formula can change from listing to listing.

That means we can't honestly rank Day Guard above or below ZBiotics. What we can do is give you a quick way to judge it, or any other hangover product you come across:

- **Read the full ingredient list.** If it hides behind a "proprietary blend" with no amounts, you can't compare doses.
- **Look up the main ingredients one by one.** Many of these products combine DHM, L-cysteine, milk thistle, prickly pear, B vitamins, and electrolytes. Each has its own (usually limited) evidence.
- **Check who makes it.** A named company with contact details and third-party testing is a better bet than an anonymous listing.
- **Be wary of big promises.** Claims that a product "blocks" hangovers, "eliminates" alcohol, or lets you drink without consequences are red flags.

If a Day Guard product you're looking at turns out to be mainly DHM, the DHM section below applies to it.

## DHM Supplements: The Most Common Switch

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*). It's the main ingredient in many of the most popular hangover supplements, and it's where a lot of former ZBiotics users end up, mostly because of price.

### Why it's a different kind of alternative

ZBiotics works in your gut. DHM is absorbed into the body and has been studied for effects on how the liver handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and on how alcohol acts in the brain. That doesn't mean it works, but it does mean DHM isn't stuck with ZBiotics's main limitation of only reaching gut acetaldehyde.

### What the evidence shows for DHM

Be honest with yourself about this part. The most cited DHM study, a 2012 paper in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues at UCLA, was done in rats. Much of the rest of the research is also animal or lab work. There is limited human data, and no large trial has shown that DHM prevents hangovers. Our [DHM vs ZBiotics comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics) walks through the two approaches side by side.

### Cost

This is where DHM stands out. A typical serving of plain DHM costs under a dollar to a couple of dollars, compared with roughly $10 to $15 for a bottle of ZBiotics. If you're going to test something on a few nights out, the cheaper option lets you do that without spending much.

### Popular DHM options

- **Plain DHM capsules** such as Double Wood or NusaPure: the simplest and cheapest way to try it.
- **DHM blends** such as No Days Wasted, Cheers Restore, Flyby, and Fuller Health After Party: DHM plus extras like L-cysteine, milk thistle, prickly pear, B vitamins, or electrolytes. Blends cost more and are harder to judge because there's more going on.

Our reviews of [Cheers Restore](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review) and [Flyby](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025) go into each one, and our [ZBiotics vs Cheers comparison](/never-hungover/zbiotics-vs-cheers) puts a DHM brand head to head with ZBiotics.

**Our take:** for most people whose main complaint about ZBiotics is cost, DHM is the most practical alternative to try. Go in with realistic expectations.

## Morning Recovery and Other DHM Drinks

If you like the ZBiotics routine of a small drink before you go out, DHM also comes in that format. Morning Recovery from More Labs is the best-known example: a small bottle built around DHM with added electrolytes and other ingredients. Our [Morning Recovery review](/never-hungover/more-labs-morning-recovery-review) covers it in detail.

The trade-off is that drinks usually cost more per serving than capsules, and you're paying partly for convenience and flavor. The evidence question is the same as for any DHM product: plausible, mostly studied in animals, with little human data.

## Korean and Japanese Hangover Drinks

Hangover drinks are a huge category in South Korea and Japan, and many contain extracts of *Hovenia dulcis*, the same tree DHM comes from, along with other herbs. They're sold in convenience stores there and increasingly in Asian grocery stores elsewhere.

They're a reasonable alternative if you like the drink format and can find them easily. Formulas vary a lot, and independent evidence for specific products is thin. Our guide to [Korean and Japanese hangover pills and drinks](/never-hungover/korean-japanese-hangover-pills) explains what's in the common ones.

## Single Ingredients With a Little Human Research

Some people skip branded products entirely and try one ingredient on its own. A few have at least small human studies:

- **Prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica).** A 2004 placebo-controlled study in *Archives of Internal Medicine* reported less nausea, dry mouth, and loss of appetite the next morning in people who took prickly pear extract before drinking. It didn't reduce overall hangover severity much, and it was small. See our [DHM vs prickly pear comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers).
- **L-cysteine.** A small randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2020 reported reductions in some hangover symptoms in healthy men. It needs confirming in larger studies.
- **NAC (N-acetylcysteine).** It helps the body make glutathione, an antioxidant involved in clearing toxins. Evidence for hangovers specifically is thin. Check with your doctor first if you take medication.

These are cheap to try, but there is no good evidence that any of them prevents a hangover.

## Electrolytes and the Free Stuff That Works Best

The least exciting alternative to ZBiotics is also the one with the best support. Hangovers track most closely with how much you drink, so these habits do more than any product on this page:

- **Drink less, and drink more slowly.** The amount of alcohol is by far the biggest factor.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol is absorbed.
- **Alternate drinks with water,** and have a glass before bed.
- **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality, and poor sleep makes the next day worse.
- **Pick lighter drinks** if dark spirits hit you harder. Congeners are one of the factors linked to worse hangovers.

Electrolyte drinks can help if you're dehydrated, but there is no good evidence that they prevent a hangover on their own. Our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing, and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) pulls the best-supported habits into one plan.

## All the ZBiotics Alternatives Side by Side

| Option | Type | What it targets | Rough cost per night | Human evidence for hangovers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ZBiotics** | Engineered probiotic drink | Acetaldehyde in the gut | $10 to $15 | Mainly company research |
| **PartySmart** | Herbal capsule | Acetaldehyde and liver (per company) | Around $1 or less | Company-backed research |
| **Myrkl** | Probiotic pill | Alcohol in the gut | Several dollars | One small company-funded trial on blood alcohol |
| **Day Guard** | Varies by seller | Unclear | Varies | None we could find |
| **Plain DHM** | Capsule | Alcohol metabolism and brain effects | Under $1 to $2 | Mostly animal studies, limited human data |
| **DHM blends and drinks** | Capsule or drink | DHM plus extras | $2 to $5+ | Same as DHM, plus small studies on some extras |
| **Prickly pear, L-cysteine** | Single ingredient | Inflammation, acetaldehyde | Low | Small individual trials |
| **Habits** | Free | The amount of alcohol itself | $0 | The strongest of anything here |

Costs are rough ranges at typical retail prices and change often. Check current prices before you buy.

## Which Alternative Fits You?

- **"ZBiotics is too expensive."** Try plain DHM or PartySmart. You'll spend a fraction as much while you find out whether a product makes any difference for you.
- **"I like the probiotic idea, but I want a pill."** Myrkl is the obvious one. Keep in mind that its trial measured blood alcohol, not hangovers.
- **"I doubt a gut-only product can do much."** Choose something absorbed into the body, like DHM, rather than another gut probiotic.
- **"I like drinking something before I go out."** A DHM drink like Morning Recovery, or a Korean Hovenia drink.
- **"I'd rather not take a genetically engineered organism."** Any of the others on this page.
- **"I just want to feel better."** Start with the habits. Add a product only if you still want to experiment.

### How to test any alternative honestly

One good morning doesn't prove anything, because hangovers vary a lot with sleep, food, and what you drank. If you try something, use it on three or four nights that are as similar as possible, with the same amount and type of drink, and compare with similar nights without it. Ask yourself whether you'd notice the difference if you didn't know what you'd taken. If you can't tell, save your money.

## Red Flags in Hangover Product Marketing

Whatever you pick, be skeptical of:

- **Claims that a product "prevents," "cures," or "eliminates" hangovers.** No product has good evidence for that.
- **Promises to lower your blood alcohol or keep you sober.** Nothing in a capsule or bottle makes it safe to drive.
- **Proprietary blends with no amounts listed.**
- **"Clinically proven" with no study named,** or studies that measured something other than hangover symptoms.
- **Pressure to drink more.** A product that makes you feel protected can lead you to drink more than you would otherwise, which defeats the purpose.

If you find you rely on something to get through drinking most days, or you've had shakes, a racing heart, or confusion the day after, that's worth talking to a doctor about, without judgment.

## The Bottom Line

- There's no ZBiotics alternative with clearly stronger evidence. Most are cheaper, and some work through a different route.
- **PartySmart** is the low-cost herbal option, backed mainly by company research.
- **Myrkl** is the probiotic rival, with one small company-funded trial that measured blood alcohol, not hangovers.
- **Day Guard** products don't have enough reliable public information to review fairly. Judge them by their labels.
- **DHM** is the most practical switch for most people because of price, with the caveat that its research is mostly in animals.
- The habits that matter most, like drinking less, eating, drinking water, and sleeping, are free and work better than any product.

If you want to try DHM as your alternative, the simplest low-cost option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and a popular blend with extra ingredients is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) (we earn a commission on these links). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Whatever you choose, treat it as an experiment on top of the basics, not a replacement for them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best alternative to ZBiotics?**

It depends on why you want to switch. If the price is the problem, a plain DHM supplement costs a fraction of ZBiotics per night and is easy to try. If you specifically want a probiotic, Myrkl is the best-known alternative, though its main study measured blood alcohol, not hangovers. If you want an herbal option, PartySmart is cheap and widely sold. None of them has strong independent proof that it prevents hangovers, so the cheapest reasonable option is a sensible place to start.

**Is PartySmart better than ZBiotics?**

Neither has clearly better evidence. PartySmart is a low-cost Ayurvedic herbal capsule from Himalaya, and ZBiotics is an expensive engineered probiotic drink. Both say they help the body deal with acetaldehyde, and both lean mainly on company-backed research. PartySmart wins easily on price and convenience. ZBiotics has the more novel, clearly described mechanism. If you're choosing on cost, PartySmart is the easier experiment.

**Is Myrkl the same as ZBiotics?**

No. Both are probiotics taken before drinking, but they aim at different targets. ZBiotics uses an engineered strain of Bacillus subtilis meant to break down acetaldehyde in the gut. Myrkl uses a blend of probiotic strains that the company says break down alcohol itself in the gut. Myrkl's key published trial was small, company-funded, and measured blood alcohol rather than how people felt the next day.

**What is Day Guard and how does it compare to ZBiotics?**

Products sold under the Day Guard name come up in searches next to ZBiotics, but we couldn't find consistent, reliable information about the formula or any published human research. Without that, there's no honest way to rank it against ZBiotics. Check the ingredient label, look up the evidence for each ingredient on its own, and be wary of claims that it blocks hangovers or lowers your blood alcohol.

**Is DHM a good alternative to ZBiotics?**

For many people it's the most practical one. DHM works through a different route (it's absorbed into the body rather than acting only in the gut), and it costs far less per night. The honest caveat is that most DHM research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human hangover data. It isn't a cure, and it's best judged by trying it on a few similar nights.

**Are there cheaper alternatives to ZBiotics that actually help?**

The cheapest things with the best support are habits, not products: drink less and more slowly, eat before you drink, alternate with water, and protect your sleep. Among products, plain DHM capsules and herbal pills like PartySmart cost a small fraction of ZBiotics per night. Electrolyte drinks help with dehydration but there is no good evidence that they prevent a hangover on their own.

**Can I take ZBiotics and DHM together?**

Many people do, and there's no known harmful interaction between them for healthy adults, since one acts in the gut and the other is absorbed. That said, nobody has studied the combination, so there is no good evidence that stacking them works better than either one. If you take prescription medicine, are pregnant, or have a weakened immune system, check with a doctor or pharmacist first.

**Do any ZBiotics alternatives lower blood alcohol or make it safe to drive?**

No. Some products, Myrkl in particular, have been marketed around lowering blood alcohol, but none of them makes it safe to drive or lets you drink more without consequences. If you've been drinking, don't drive, whatever you took beforehand.
